{
  "lesson_key": "tac-1-hello-agentic-coding",
  "title": "Hello Agentic Coding",
  "course": "TAC",
  "order": 1,
  "lesson_url": "https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding/course/hello-agentic-coding",
  "video": {
    "file": "tac-1-hello-agentic-coding/video/tac-1-hello-agentic-coding.mp4",
    "duration_seconds": 1311,
    "duration_display": "21:51"
  },
  "tactic": {
    "name": "Stop Coding",
    "one_liner": "Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code — hand the typing to agents and move your engineering cycles up the stack.",
    "why_uncomfortable": "It asks career engineers to retire the skill that defined them. Dan spent over a decade at startups and large companies typing code by hand — mastering languages, syntax, algorithms, data structures — and says he misses it too. The tactic demands you trust that language models running in agentic loops on supercomputers are now vastly superior coders, and that clinging to hand-typing means you have no chance of keeping up. Evolution forces us to leave skills behind to adopt new ones."
  },
  "mission": "Transform you into an engineer they can't replace — 'they' being your boss, the company, the industry, and AI itself. In a world where code is a commodity and your grandma or little brother can build an app with one prompt, you become irreplaceable the way engineers always have in technological revolutions: move up the stack. Become a commander of compute that builds systems that build systems, until your codebase runs itself.",
  "phase_model": {
    "phase1_ai_coding": "The generative-AI age's first phase: prompt-to-generate-code. Birth of vibe coders and the complete commoditization of code. You interact with the big three — context, model, prompt — to build faster than ever. Still foundational, no longer differentiating.",
    "phase2_agentic_coding": "Where real engineers strike back. A superset of AI coding: the big three plus tools — prompts that reliably execute long chains of tool calls inside an agentic coding tool. Engineers reallocate their cycles to planning, reviewing, and creating closed-loop structures, and turn their codebases into increasingly self-operating machines."
  },
  "core_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "agentic-engineer",
      "name": "The Agentic Engineer — a new role",
      "plain_english": "A software engineer whose job is not writing code but building systems that can take actions the way an engineer would: branch, write, run, test, commit, report. Dan bought agenticengineer.com in 2023 betting this role would emerge; lesson 1 declares it now exists.",
      "dan_words": "\"Predicting that a new role of software engineering would emerge, defined by the ability to build systems that can take actions as we can. It's become clear this new role now exists.\"",
      "misconception": "That 'agentic engineer' is a rebrand of 'prompt engineer.' It isn't: the role is defined by system-building (embedding agents across the SDLC), not by writing clever one-off prompts."
    },
    {
      "id": "phase-one-vs-phase-two",
      "name": "Phase 1 (AI coding) vs Phase 2 (agentic coding)",
      "plain_english": "Phase 1 = using AI to generate code faster (context, model, prompt). Phase 2 = using AI to perform engineering work end-to-end (add tools). The lesson's entire arc is the delta between these two phases, demonstrated with two prompts in one README.",
      "dan_words": "\"In the generative AI age, AI coding was phase one. Here we saw the birth of VibeCoders and the complete commoditization of code... Agentic coding marks phase two. This is where real engineers strike back.\"",
      "misconception": "That phase 2 replaces phase 1 knowledge. Agentic coding is a superset of AI coding — the big three are still there, always, even when you can't see them."
    },
    {
      "id": "stop-coding",
      "name": "Tactic #1: Stop Coding",
      "plain_english": "Stop typing code by hand. Not stop shipping code, not stop reading code — stop being the instrument that types it. Use the best tool for the job: agentic loops running powerful language models. Throughout all of TAC, not a single line of code is typed by hand.",
      "dan_words": "\"Let's end the debate right now. Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code, full stop.\"",
      "misconception": "Two opposite failure readings: (1) 'so we don't generate code anymore' — wrong, code is still a primary asset and you'll generate more than ever; (2) 'so I can stop understanding code' — wrong, code understanding is still critically important. What ends is hand-typing, and what replaces it is planning, reviewing, and closed-loop structures."
    },
    {
      "id": "commander-of-compute",
      "name": "Commander of Compute",
      "plain_english": "The identity shift of phase 2: your job is deciding where compute gets aimed and what systems it builds, not producing keystrokes. You don't just prompt to generate code — you direct compute to build systems that build systems.",
      "dan_words": "\"We move up the stack once again. We become a commander of compute... You take this compute and you use it to build systems that build systems.\"",
      "misconception": "That commanding compute means firing off more prompts manually. The command is structural — triggers, scripts, workflows that fire agents at the right time — not a human clicking faster."
    },
    {
      "id": "big-three",
      "name": "The Big Three (context, model, prompt)",
      "plain_english": "The three primitives of phase-1 AI coding: what the model can see (context), which model does the work (model), and what you ask for (prompt). Every AI coding interaction is governed by these whether you notice or not.",
      "dan_words": "\"With AI coding, you've been interacting with the big three: context, model, prompt. This is a principle of AI coding. It's always there even if you can't see it.\"",
      "misconception": "That the big three become obsolete in phase 2. They remain the foundation; phase 2 adds exactly one new dimension on top."
    },
    {
      "id": "core-four",
      "name": "The Core Four (context, model, prompt, tools)",
      "plain_english": "Add tools to the big three and you get the core four — the primitives of agentic coding. The 'tools' element specifically means prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tool calls, not the mere existence of tool calling.",
      "dan_words": "\"The new element that transforms the big three of AI coding to Agentic Coding is prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tools. When you add tools, we upgrade the big three to the core four.\"",
      "misconception": "'Tool calling has been around for a while, this is not new.' Dan's rebuttal: you're 100% right — and it's not a question of new, it's a question of scale and performance. Reliable long-chain execution is what changed."
    },
    {
      "id": "agentic-prompt",
      "name": "The Agentic (Coding) Prompt",
      "plain_english": "A prompt that contains a sequence of tool calls — a workflow specification, not a text request. It reads like a runbook (RUN / CREATE / RUN / REPORT) and executes like one: branch, write files, run programs, commit, report. It is the unit of engineering work in TAC, and every later lesson scales it.",
      "dan_words": "\"Everything we do in TAC is built upon this core idea you can see right in this readme with just 35 lines... A prompt contains a sequence of tool calls.\"",
      "misconception": "That it's 'just a prompt' — everyone knows prompts can call tools now. People don't invest the time to understand what this means at scale: fired repeatedly, with the right triggers and leverage, one prompt becomes an end-to-end developer workflow running minutes to hours without you."
    },
    {
      "id": "claude-code-form-factor",
      "name": "Claude Code's three essential elements",
      "plain_english": "Claude Code is the first agentic coding tool to properly combine: (1) a powerful language model that can reason when needed, (2) the ability to consistently call long chains of tools, and (3) the right agent architecture. That combination — being copied by every other tool — unlocks the core four, which unlocks the agentic prompt.",
      "dan_words": "\"Claude Code is the first Agentic Coding tool to properly combine three essential elements: a powerful language model that can reason when needed, the ability to consistently call long chains of tools, and the right agent architecture... Reliable Agentic Coding at scale was not possible before Claude Code.\"",
      "misconception": "That the lesson is Claude Code marketing and expires with the tool. Dan pre-handles this: your UI may differ, your models will be newer — great. The tactics are transferable to any tool with the right capabilities; don't get stuck on any one tool."
    },
    {
      "id": "programmable-agentic-coding",
      "name": "Programmable agentic coding (claude -p)",
      "plain_english": "Because Claude Code runs in the terminal, any language with terminal access can invoke it as a function: read a prompt file, pass it to `claude -p`, capture the output. The repo shows the identical pattern in shell, TypeScript+Bun, and Python+UV. The agent stops being a chat window and becomes a component you embed anywhere in the software development lifecycle.",
      "dan_words": "\"Claude Code is also a programmable Agentic Coding tool... we can run it from any programming language that has terminal access... we can embed our own agents, our own workflows, our own agentic prompts across the software development lifecycle.\"",
      "misconception": "That the demo scripts are trivial wrappers not worth running ('I already watched Dan do it'). The scripts ARE the lesson: it's not just about the agentic prompt, it's about where you can use it — including full agentic environments where you're not even present."
    },
    {
      "id": "systems-that-build-systems",
      "name": "Systems that build systems / self-operating codebase",
      "plain_english": "The end-state: codebases that increasingly run themselves — agents firing at the right time, doing the right work, with and without your oversight. Lesson 1 plants the seed (a scripted agent that does a full branch-write-run-commit-report cycle); the rest of TAC scales it.",
      "dan_words": "\"The irreplaceable engineer in phase two that we're aiming to become is the engineer that transforms their code bases into self-operating machines... so much so that your code base literally runs itself.\"",
      "misconception": "That this is hype about full autonomy tomorrow. The lesson's actual claim is incremental: 'increasingly self-operating,' built by investing your time in the right places and repeatedly extracting value."
    },
    {
      "id": "engineer-not-coder",
      "name": "You're an engineer, not a coder",
      "plain_english": "Engineering was never about writing code; it's about building systems of leverage that produce valuable outcomes for users and customers. Code is one asset those systems produce. This reframe is what makes 'stop coding' coherent rather than self-destructive.",
      "dan_words": "\"Engineering was never about writing code. It's about building systems of leverage that produce valuable outcomes for your users and your customers... Remember, you're an engineer, not a coder. The difference is massive.\"",
      "misconception": "That leverage means working more hours with AI. The 10x engineer emerges from 10x leverage, not 10x time or effort — and the number is arbitrary (2x, 10x, 100x) depending on the leverage points you find."
    },
    {
      "id": "replace-yourself",
      "name": "To become irreplaceable, replace yourself",
      "plain_english": "The lesson's closing paradox: the engineer who systematically automates their own work (replaces themselves) becomes the one the org can't replace — because they're the one who builds and commands the automation. Vibe coders can't replicate this.",
      "dan_words": "\"The contradicting truth about what you'll learn in tactical agentic coding is this: To become an irreplaceable engineer, you will replace yourself.\"",
      "misconception": "Reading it as job-loss fatalism. It's the opposite — an asymmetric-advantage strategy: in the tech industry, all the alpha lies in the future, in pushing what's possible forward."
    }
  ],

content.content:
1	# Pi Verifier Agent
2	
3	> A two-agent system with a custom pi agent harness that treats verification as a first-class problem, not an additional human-in-the-loop workflow.
4	
5	![Pi Verifier Agent — animated two-agent observer architecture: engineer prompts the BUILDER, BUILDER writes session.jsonl, VERIFIER reads the session JSONL and prompts corrections back to BUILDER, all under a defense-in-depth bash and persona policy](./images/arch-loop.svg)
6	
7	## How it works
8	
9	A two-agent observer system for the [Pi Coding Agent](https://pi.dev): a normal interactive **Builder** runs in your terminal; a sibling **Verifier** Pi runs in its own tmux window with input disabled. After every builder turn, the verifier independently re-runs the work using deterministic read-only tools and prompts the builder back with concrete corrective feedback when verification fails. It closes the review-constraint feedback loop so you can stop hand-checking every "✅ done."
10	
11	## Quick start
12	
13	### Agentic Installation
14	
15	Open Claude Code or Pi Coding Agent (or any coding agent you want)
16	
17	```bash
18	/install              # one-time — open Claude Code in this repo and run it
19	```
20	
21	Then run
22	
23	```bash
24	just v             # boot a generic verifier; or `just vpy` for python, `just vimg` for gpt-image-2, `just vsql` for a sqlite verifier
25	```
26	
27	### Manual Installation
28	
29	No Claude Code? See [Manual install (no agentic coding tool)](#manual-install-no-agentic-coding-tool) below.
30	
31	### What you'll see on Startup:
32	
33	![Two-agent runtime — builder Pi on the left, verifier Pi on the right, communicating over a unix domain socket while the verifier observes the builder's session JSONL](./images/verifier.png)
34	
35	1. The builder Pi opens in your current terminal. The default footer is hidden; instead, the **input box's borders carry the live status**:
36	   - Top-right border: `● verifier connected` (or `◌ spawning`, `✗ disconnected`, `⚠ error`)
37	   - Bottom-left border: active model id (e.g. `claude-sonnet-4-6`)
38	   - Bottom-right border: context-window utilization (e.g. `12%`)
39	2. **A new OS-level terminal window opens automatically.** If you're already inside `$TMUX`, you get a sibling tmux window instead. If your `$TERM_PROGRAM` is recognized (Ghostty / iTerm / Apple_Terminal / WezTerm), the launcher targets that emulator directly; otherwise it falls back to a Terminal.app window via `osascript do script` so engineers always see a real window — never a headless tmux session.
40	3. The verifier window comes pre-tuned: **mouse scroll enabled**, **bottom green tmux status bar hidden**, **10k-line scrollback**, **OSC52 clipboard** (mouse-drag → Cmd+V works natively). Tmux defaults are session-scoped — your other tmux sessions are untouched.
41	4. The verifier's input row is replaced by a colored full-width status bar — input is locked. The bar shows `VERIFIER · <phase> · <CONFIDENCE>` and updates live (e.g. `VERIFIER · ✓ verified · PERFECT`). The bar's **background color reflects the confidence grade**: green for PERFECT/VERIFIED, orange for PARTIAL/FEEDBACK, red for FAILED, purple while idle/verifying.
42	5. Type a normal builder prompt. After the builder finishes its turn, the verifier auto-runs verification.
43	6. If verification fails, the verifier calls `verifier_prompt` with concrete corrective feedback. The builder receives it as a follow-up user message (via `pi.sendUserMessage(deliverAs:"followUp")`) and runs another turn fixing the issue.
44	7. Loop repeats up to `max_loops: 3` (configurable per persona). On the 4th attempt, the builder surfaces an "escalating to human" message instead of auto-injecting another correction.
45	8. On `Ctrl+D` of the builder, the verifier window closes, the unix socket is unlinked, and the breadcrumb at `.pi/state/verifier-<sid>.sock.ref` is cleaned up. (`just clean` also force-tears-down anything stale from a prior crash.)
46	
47	## What this two-agent system does
48	
49	Engineers spend roughly half their time reviewing agent output. Every "I created the table," "I added the foreign key," "I applied the migration" has to be re-checked by hand. That review work is the binding constraint on agentic engineering throughput. The Pi Verifier Agent moves it onto a second agent.
50	
51	The pattern is a **top-down observer**: the builder *doesn't know* the verifier exists. The verifier connects to the builder over a unix domain socket, listens for the builder's lifecycle ticks (`start` / `stop` / `error`), pulls the full transcript from the builder's session JSONL on disk, and runs verification through a single allowlisted astral-uv script (see `.pi/verifier/scripts/verify_python.py` for v1). When verification fails, the verifier calls its `verifier_prompt` tool — the only thing it can do that touches the builder — and the builder injects the message via `pi.sendUserMessage(deliverAs: "followUp")` and runs another turn. The loop repeats up to three times, then escalates to the human.
52	
53	The verifier is **read-only by architecture**, not by prompt. Its persona declares no `write` or `edit` tools. Its bash policy is `mode: script-only` — every `bash` call is checked at the tool-call level and blocked unless it starts with the allowed runner + script. The script itself opens SQLite databases with `mode=ro&immutable=1` so even a mutation that somehow slipped through would be refused at the connection layer. Three independent layers (persona tools list, bash override, read-only DB connection) all have to be defeated before anything mutates state.
54	
55	The verifier's job is orchestrating deterministic (and non-deterministic) checks; the agentic part is just glue. When verification can't be done — no oracle, no fixture, no script subcommand — the verifier explicitly says *"this is what I'd need from you to verify this next time."* That gap becomes the next thing you template into the script. *Verifier accuracy compounds.*
56	
57	## What this unlocks
58	
59	The verifier doubles your tokens per turn to give you two things one agent can't:
60	
61	1. **Verification** — proof the builder did what it claimed.
62	2. **Review** — proof what got built is what you actually asked for.
63	
64	If you optimize for tokens, this looks wasteful. If you optimize for *time*, it's the highest-leverage trade you can make. Tokens are cheap. Your time is not. Spend tokens to generate value and time.
65	
66	This is the rare pattern that compounds on **both trust and scale**. Most agentic systems force a tradeoff between the two — review more deeply and you slow down (scale ↓), push more compute through the system and you erode the trust you have in any single output (trust ↓). The verifier doesn't trade. It scales the work (the verifier often burns 2–5× the builder's tokens per turn) AND increases trust (every atomic claim now has a deterministic check behind it before you ever read "✅ done"). More work + more proof. Both axes, simultaneously.
67	
68	### The review constraint of agentic engineering
69	
70	Agentic engineering has two binding constraints: **how much you can plan**, and **how much you can review**. Most engineers stall on review — half their day is spent re-checking "I created the table" / "I added the FK" / "I applied the migration" by hand. The verifier collapses that side of the constraint into a parallel agent whose entire job is re-checking, deterministically, with read-only tools.
71	
72	The other side — planning — most engineers under-invest in. The verifier compounds there too: every claim it can't verify becomes an explicit ask ("you'd need a fixture for this next time"), which feeds back into the next iteration of the script and persona. The bottleneck stops being you.
73	
74	A common objection: "won't adding agents just increase the error rate?" Only if you don't engineer them. With the right **core four** — context, model, prompt, tools — and full control over the agent harness, the math flips. You open the same agentic coding tool everyone else opens. Your results are different. Your results are *verified*.
75	
76	### Template your verification engineering
77	
78	The verifier is structurally un-promptable. Its input bar is locked; you cannot drop one-off instructions into it. The only thing that drives it is `verify_on_stop.md` rendered against the builder's `stop` event.
79	
80	That sounds annoying. It's the point.
81	
82	You can't fix bugs by typing at the verifier — you fix them by editing the persona, the script, or the prompt template. Improvements solve the entire problem class, not the one instance you happened to hit. Every gap turns into reusable engineering. One-off prompts solve the instance; templated verification solves the class.
83	
84	The lock isn't friction-for-friction's-sake. It's the mechanism that makes templated engineering a habit *by force*. When the only available action is "improve the persona, script, or template," that's the action you take — every time. The lowest-hanging fruit of the generative-AI age (fire a one-off prompt and move on) is removed from the menu. What's left is the work that compounds.
85	
86	This is how you build the system that builds the system.
87	
88	### Two coordinated agents will always beat one
89	
90	![Two camps — CAMP A (engineer stuck in prompt → babysit → re-prompt loop) vs CAMP B (BUILDER + VERIFIER coordinated, build · verify · feedback · repeat)](./images/07-two-camps.svg)
91	
92	Look closely at any model benchmark — Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, DeepSeek V4, GLM 5.1, Kimi K2.6, the Qwen series. They all make the same mistake from an engineer's perspective: each model is evaluated **in isolation**. The real frontier of intelligence isn't picking the best model. It's combinations. The right answer to "Opus 4.7 or GPT-5.5?" is **and**, not **or**. Stack them. Coordinate them. Specialize them. That's the move benchmarks can't measure but you can build.
93	
94	A single agent reviewing its own output is one perspective at one moment in compute. Two coordinated agents give you a second perspective, doubled compute, and a hard architectural separation between writing and checking. The verifier has tools the builder doesn't (a domain script, a read-only persona). The builder has affordances the verifier doesn't (write, edit, generate). They don't compete; they specialize.
95	
96	The trade is always the same: more tokens for more time back. If you can pay tokens to reclaim hours, take that trade every time. Your time is your most valuable resource — full stop.
97	
98	### Specialized prompts at scale
99	
100	The verifier sees the **original user prompt** via the builder's `start` event — the prompt you typed becomes part of the verifier's per-cycle context. Write claim-style prompts ("create the users table with these exact constraints, FKs to `org`, NOT NULL on `email`") and the verifier picks them up automatically as atomic propositions to check.
101	
102	That changes what kind of prompt is worth writing. You stop writing prompts an agent might *do* and start writing specs an *engineered system* can verify. Plans. Contracts. Scaled prompts that do work no one else's stack can do — because you specialized yours.
103	
104	## Architecture overview
105	
106	```
107	   ┌──────────────────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────────────┐
108	   │  Your Terminal               │         │  New OS Window  (or sibling  │
109	   │  (Ghostty / iTerm / ...)     │         │   tmux window if in $TMUX)   │
110	   │                              │         │                              │
111	   │  ┌────────────────────────┐  │         │  ┌────────────────────────┐  │
112	   │  │  pi  (BUILDER)         │  │         │  │  pi  (VERIFIER --child)│  │
113	   │  │  verifiable.ts         │◄─┼─unix────┼─►│  verifier.ts           │  │
114	   │  │  + socket server       │  │ socket  │  │  + status-bar editor   │  │
115	   │  │  + lifecycle forwarder │  │ JSONL   │  │  + bash override       │  │
116	   │  └─────────┬──────────────┘  │         │  │  + verifier_prompt tool│  │
117	   │            │                 │         │  └─────────┬──────────────┘  │
118	   └────────────┼─────────────────┘         └────────────┼─────────────────┘
119	                │                                        │
120	                │ writes session JSONL                   │ reads
121	                ▼                                        ▼
122	        ~/.pi/agent/sessions/<sid>.jsonl  ──────────────►   (builder transcript)
123	
124	        ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
125	        verifier's only bash command:
126	            uv run --script .pi/verifier/scripts/verify_sqlite.py <db> "<sqlite3 cmd>"
127	        ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
128	```
129	
130	One Pi binary, two roles. The builder owns a unix domain socket at `/tmp/pi-verifier/<sessionId>.sock` (short path so we sidestep macOS's 104-byte `sun_path` limit). The builder pushes lifecycle ticks only — never transcript content. The verifier pulls the substantive content it needs from the builder's session JSONL on disk and runs verification through the script.
131	
132	### Direction matrix
133	
134	The wire protocol is asymmetric — the verifier originates connection setup and corrective prompts; the builder pushes lifecycle events. Direction is enforced by `assertDirection()` in [`apps/verifier/_shared/ipc.ts`](./apps/verifier/_shared/ipc.ts):
135	
136	```
137	verifier ──► builder           builder ──► verifier
138	─────────────────────          ──────────────────────
139	hello                          hello_ack            ← handshake
140	prompt   (correction text)     prompt_ack           ← receipt confirmation
141	report   (rendered inline)     (no reply needed)    ← informational
142	                               event                ← unified lifecycle channel
143	
144	Bidirectional (both sides may send):
145	  ping / pong  — both run a 10s liveness interval and reply to the peer's pings
146	  bye          — either side may initiate a clean teardown
147	```
148	
149	All envelopes are TypeScript discriminated unions on `type`, JSONL-framed (one JSON object per line, terminated by `\n` — split on `\n` only, never via Node's `readline` which would split on `U+2028` / `U+2029` embedded in JSON strings).
150	
151	### Verifier state machine
152	
153	```
154	                    ┌────────────────┐
155	                    │   connecting   │  ← session_start; net.createConnection
156	                    └────────┬───────┘
157	                             │ hello_ack
158	                             ▼
159	                    ┌────────────────┐
160	              ┌────►│   connected    │
161	              │     └────────┬───────┘
162	              │              │ event {name:"stop"}
163	              │              ▼
164	              │     ┌────────────────┐
165	              │     │   verifying    │
166	              │     └────────┬───────┘
167	              │              │ verifier's own agent_end → parseReport
168	              │              ▼
169	              │  ┌─────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
170	              │  ▼         ▼         ▼         ▼
171	              │ verified  failed   unsure    error
172	              │  │         │         │       (parse fail / no msg)
173	              │  └─────────┴─────────┴───────────┘
174	              │  next event {name:"start"} resets to connected
175	              │
176	              │     ┌────────────────┐
177	              └─────│  disconnected  │  ← socket close → 5s grace → ctx.shutdown()
178	                    └────────────────┘
179	```
180	
181	The builder side keeps a simpler footer state: `idle` / `disconnected` / `spawning` / `connected` / `error`. It also tracks `loopCount` per genuine user prompt; on `loopCount > maxLoops` the next `prompt` is rejected with `prompt_ack { ok:false, error:"max loops exceeded" }` and the builder surfaces a `verifier-escalation` system message.

185	Claude Code (or any agentic coding tool that can read and execute `.claude/commands/`) is the bootloader for this system. Open your agentic coding tool in this repo and run a single command to walk through the entire setup process:

188	/install

193	- **Node 20+** and `npm`
194	- **Python 3.11+** (the verifier script uses an inline PEP 723 `# /// script` header)

245	### `.env`
246	
247	Both the builder and the verifier load `.env` from your **current working directory** on `session_start` (using Node's built-in `process.loadEnvFile`). The verifier inherits the builder's env via tmux `-e KEY=VAL` flags AND independently loads `.env` from the same cwd as a defensive backstop — tmux's "new sessions inherit the server's env" behavior is unreliable when a tmux server is already running, so we don't trust it.
248	
249	What this means: drop your provider API keys (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, etc.) into a project-local `.env` and **both agents see them automatically** — no shell-config gymnastics required. Existing `process.env` always wins; `.env` only fills gaps.
250	
251	> `OPENAI_API_KEY` is also what powers the [`gpt-image-2` skill](#image-verifier-demo-the-gpt-image-2-skill) used in the `just vimg` demo — see below.

276	### Image-verifier demo: the `gpt-image-2` skill
277	
278	The `just vimg` recipe pairs with a Claude Code skill at [`.claude/skills/gpt-image-2/`](./.claude/skills/gpt-image-2/) — that's what the **builder** invokes to actually generate or edit images. The verifier persona ([`.pi/verifier/agents/verify_image.md`](./.pi/verifier/agents/verify_image.md)) is vision-capable, so it inspects the resulting file and decides whether the image matches the original prompt. Together they form the demo: builder generates → verifier looks at the pixels → verifier prompts a correction if the output drifts.
279	
280	To run the demo end-to-end you need `OPENAI_API_KEY` set. Drop it into your project-local `.env` and both Pi processes pick it up automatically — same `.env` mechanism that handles your verifier-model API key. No other shell config required.
281	
282	The skill is also what we used to generate the architecture animation embedded at the top of this README (`images/arch-loop.svg`), so it doubles as a general image-authoring helper inside any Claude Code session running in this repo.
283	
284	A worked example from a recent run: the builder generated an architecture diagram via the skill. The verifier read the resulting file, decomposed the user's prompt into atomic visual claims (image exists, depicts the verifier two-agent system, **≤10 distinct text blocks per the persona's readability contract**, text legible at 1× scale), and discovered the diagram was overloaded with text — fourteen blocks, violating the readability rule baked into `verify_image.md`. It called `verifier_prompt` with concrete corrective feedback ("regenerate with fewer text blocks; the current draft has 14"). The builder ran a second turn, generated a cleaner diagram, and the next verification cycle came back `STATUS: VERIFIED · CONFIDENCE: PERFECT`. The human never touched the keyboard for the correction. The rule lives in the persona; the verifier enforces it on every image, every cycle, forever.
285	
286	### The CONFIDENCE ladder
287	
288	The verifier's persona instructs the agent to emit a `CONFIDENCE:` line under `STATUS:` on every Report. The grade encodes both completeness AND outcome:
289	
290	| Level | Meaning | Bar color |
291	|---|---|---|
292	| `PERFECT` | Every claim verified, zero gaps, no feedback | 🟢 green |
293	| `VERIFIED` | All checked passed, minor non-blocking gaps | 🟢 green |
294	| `PARTIAL` | No failures, but significant unverifiable gaps | 🟠 orange |
295	| `FEEDBACK` | At least one claim failed, `verifier_prompt` called (system working as designed) | 🟠 orange |
296	| `FAILED` | Couldn't verify at all — escalating to human | 🔴 red |
297	
298	If the agent omits the `CONFIDENCE:` line, the parser derives a fallback from STATUS so the bar always has a meaningful color.
299	
300	## How it works mid-level details (1-min version)
301	
302	- On `session_start`, the builder extension (`verifiable.ts`) runs `spawnVerifierChild()`. The launcher branches on `$TMUX`: if set, it creates the verifier as a sibling tmux window; if not, it creates a detached tmux session and opens a new OS window attached to it (per-emulator dispatch for Ghostty / iTerm / Terminal.app / WezTerm / gnome-terminal / konsole / kitty / alacritty / xterm).
303	- The builder owns a unix domain socket at `/tmp/pi-verifier/<sessionId>.sock`. The verifier connects, sends `hello`, waits for `hello_ack`.
304	- The builder forwards lifecycle ticks as `event` envelopes: `before_agent_start` → `start`, `agent_end` → `stop`, uncaught errors → `error`. No transcript content crosses the socket.
305	- On `stop`, the verifier renders a `🪝 builder event · stop · turn N · <iso>` system message in its scrollback, templates `.pi/verifier/prompts/verify_on_stop.md` with the turn metadata, and injects it via `pi.sendUserMessage`. The verifier's persona body tells it to read the builder's session JSONL, identify claims, and run the script.
306	- If verification fails, the verifier calls `verifier_prompt(session_id, message)`. That tool writes a `prompt` envelope to the parent socket and waits for `prompt_ack` (60s timeout). The builder calls `pi.sendUserMessage(message, { deliverAs: "followUp" })`.
307	- On the verifier's own `agent_end`, the extension parses the `## Report` block out of the last assistant message (extracts STATUS + CONFIDENCE + sections), ships it to the builder as a `report` envelope. The builder stashes it for max-loops escalation but does NOT echo it inline — the full Report is already visible in the verifier's window, and the builder side only needs the metadata. The verifier reads only the relevant slice of the builder's session JSONL using `<SESSION_FILE_START_LINE>`–`<SESSION_FILE_END_LINE>` line offsets passed in the `stop` event, so it doesn't scan the whole (possibly multi-MB) session file each cycle.
308	
309	## How to author a new domain verifier
310	
311	The pattern is two files per domain. Cloning is intentional — keep the script and the persona side-by-side so the bash policy and the script's CLI shape stay in sync.
312	
313	1. **Clone the script.** Start from `.pi/verifier/scripts/verify_sqlite.py`. Keep the shebang `#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run --script`, the `# /// script` PEP 723 header, the `emit()` / `reject()` helpers, and the `main()` argparse skeleton. Replace the SQLite-specific routing (dot-commands / `SELECT` / `PRAGMA`) with whatever your domain needs:
314	   - HTTP / deploy verifier: probe endpoints with `httpx` or `urllib`; assert status codes, response shapes.
315	   - Playwright UI verifier: take screenshots, run accessibility snapshots, assert presence of expected DOM.
316	   - Type / coverage verifier: shell out to `mypy` / `tsc` / `coverage` and parse their output.
317	   Keep the rejection contract: every refusal prints a structured JSON object with `error`, `received`, `reason`, `allowed`, `hint` and exits non-zero. The agent reads that JSON as the bash tool result and self-corrects on the next step — *the error message is the documentation*.
318	2. **Clone the persona.** Start from `.pi/verifier/agents/verify_sqlite.md`. Update the frontmatter:
319	   ```yaml
320	   ---
321	   name: verify-<domain>
322	   description: <domain> verifier — <what it checks>. Read-only.
323	   tools: read, grep, find, ls, bash
324	   model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6
325	   domain: <domain>
326	   max_loops: 3
327	   bash_policy:
328	     mode: script-only
329	     allowed_script: .pi/verifier/scripts/verify_<domain>.py
330	     runner: "uv run --script"
331	   verification_focus:
332	     - <focus area 1>
333	     - <focus area 2>
334	   ---
335	   ```
336	   Body: keep the meta-prompt 6-section structure (Purpose / Variables / Codebase Structure / Instructions / Workflow / Report). Update `### Tool policy` and `### Verification heuristics` for your domain. Keep the placeholders `<BUILDER_SESSION_ID>`, `<BUILDER_SESSION_FILE>`, `<DOMAIN>`, `<MAX_LOOPS>`, `<SOCKET_PATH>` — they're filled at spawn time. Keep the literal `## Report` block and the `STATUS:` line — the verifier extension parses it.
337	3. **Wire it in.** v1 hardcodes `.pi/verifier/agents/verify_sqlite.md` as the agent path in `verifiable.ts` (`attach()`); to drive a different domain today, point that constant at your new persona, or pass your own with the `/verify` slash command. A `--verifier-agent` flag is on the post-v1 list.
338	
339	The `verify_on_stop.md` user-prompt template stays the same across domains — it just templates `<TURN_INDEX>` and `<TIMESTAMP>` and tells the agent to follow its system-prompt workflow.
340	
341	## Agent security: how the bash tool is locked down
342	
343	The verifier is **read-only by architecture**, not by prompt. An LLM that decides to run `rm -rf` does not get to. There is no clever jailbreak that unlocks `INSERT` for the SQLite verifier or `pip install` for the Python verifier — the policy is enforced *outside* the model.
344	
345	There are **three independent layers** between the verifier's LLM and your filesystem. All three would have to fail before any state mutates:
346	
347	### Layer 1 — persona tool allowlist (no `write`, no `edit`)
348	
349	Every domain persona declares its `tools:` field as `read, grep, find, ls, bash, verifier_prompt` — and *only* those. The launcher passes that exact list to `pi --tools`, which means Pi's runtime tool registry simply does not register `write`, `edit`, or any mutation-capable tool for the verifier process. The model can't call what isn't there.
350	
351	```yaml
352	# .pi/verifier/agents/verify_sqlite.md
353	tools: read, grep, find, ls, bash, verifier_prompt
354	```
355	
356	The `verifier_prompt` tool is registered by the verifier extension itself and is the *only* outbound channel back to the builder — see [`apps/verifier/verifier.ts`](./apps/verifier/verifier.ts). It writes a `prompt` envelope to the parent socket; it cannot touch your files.
357	
358	### Layer 2 — bash policy override (script-only)
359	
360	`bash` is the one tool in the allowlist that *could* mutate state. We narrow it at the tool-call level via `pi.on("tool_call")` returning `{ block: true, reason }` for any invocation that doesn't match the persona's declared `bash_policy`.
361	
362	```yaml
363	# .pi/verifier/agents/verify_sqlite.md
364	bash_policy:
365	  mode: script-only
366	  allowed_script: .pi/verifier/scripts/verify_sqlite.py
367	  runner: "uv run --script"
368	```
369	
370	The hook is in [`apps/verifier/verifier.ts`](./apps/verifier/verifier.ts) (search for `bash_policy`):
371	
372	```ts
373	const expected = `${state.bashPolicy.runner} ${state.bashPolicy.allowed_script}`;
374	if (cmd.startsWith(expected)) return; // allow.
375	return {
376	  block: true,
377	  reason: "Bash is restricted to the verifier script. ..."
378	};
379	```
380	
381	A blocked command is *not* a silent failure. The block reason is fed back to the model as a structured teaching message that names the allowed form, lists examples, and tells the agent how to reformulate. The agent reads its own error and self-corrects on the next step. **The error message is the documentation.**
382	
383	Per-domain enforcement today:
384	
385	| Persona              | bash_policy           | Allowed bash invocations                                                                       |
386	| -------------------- | --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
387	| `verify_sqlite.md`   | `script-only`         | `uv run --script .pi/verifier/scripts/verify_sqlite.py <db> "<sqlite3 command>"`               |
388	| `verify_python.md`   | `script-only`         | `uv run --script .pi/verifier/scripts/verify_python.py <subcommand> ...`                        |
389	| `verify_image.md`    | none (vision-only)    | Pi default bash surface — vision is the oracle; the persona body is the policy.                |
390	| `verifier.md` (generic) | none               | Pi default bash surface — the generic persona doesn't yet know which subcommands it'll need.   |
391	
392	For the two personas that ship with `bash_policy`, every `bash` call **must** start with the exact `runner allowed_script` prefix. `cat /etc/passwd`, `psql`, `python -c "..."`, `sh -c '...'` — all blocked at the hook layer before they reach any subprocess.
393	
394	### Layer 3 — the script itself enforces read-only
395	
396	Even if the bash override were bypassed (e.g. by loading a malicious persona that overrides `allowed_script`), the script that *does* run is engineered to refuse mutations:
397	
398	- **`verify_sqlite.py`** — opens the database with `sqlite3.connect(f"file:{path}?mode=ro&immutable=1", uri=True)`. SQLite itself refuses any write attempt at the connection layer. Dot-commands route through `sqlite3 -readonly <db>`. The script also enforces a **PRAGMA allowlist** — only introspective PRAGMAs (`integrity_check`, `foreign_key_list`, `foreign_key_check`, `index_list`, `index_info`, `table_info`, `table_xinfo`, `database_list`, `schema_version`, `user_version`) are accepted. Mutation-capable PRAGMAs like `writable_schema` and `journal_mode` are refused with a structured JSON error.
399	- **`verify_python.py`** — runs `uvx ty`, `uvx ruff check`, `uvx ruff format --check`, `uv run pytest --collect-only` / `pytest`. Each invocation is a pinned subprocess against tool binaries that don't mutate source files (or in the case of `format --check`, deliberately runs in check-only mode).
400	
401	Every refusal returns a structured JSON object `{ error, received, reason, allowed, hint }` and exits non-zero. Same teaching contract as Layer 2: the agent reads the rejection and self-corrects.
402	
403	### What this means in practice
404	
405	Three layers — persona `tools:` allowlist, bash policy override, read-only script — all have to be defeated before anything mutates state. The first two run **before** any subprocess starts; the third runs inside a process whose only filesystem reach is what its CLI argparse accepts.
406	
407	```
408	LLM decides to run a command
409	         │
410	         ▼
411	[Layer 1] Pi's tool registry — persona tools: list
412	         │   tools not in the list don't exist for this process
413	         ▼
414	[Layer 2] tool_call hook — bash_policy.allowed_script
415	         │   non-matching bash → block + teaching message
416	         ▼
417	[Layer 3] verify_*.py — argparse + ro-mode subprocess
418	         │   non-allowlisted action → structured JSON rejection
419	         ▼
420	   Allowed read-only operation runs
421	```
422	
423	### Other security boundaries
424	
425	- **Unix socket dir is `chmod 0700`.** The `/tmp/pi-verifier/` directory is created with mode 0700, so only the owning UID can connect to sockets inside it. That is the authentication — no token, no shared secret, nothing to leak in `ps`.
426	- **Defense-in-depth input lock.** The verifier replaces its editor with a `CustomEditor` subclass that swallows typing, *and* `pi.on("input")` rejects any non-extension-source input. Two independent layers prevent human keystrokes from driving the verifier — the only thing that drives it is `verify_on_stop.md` rendered against the builder's `stop` event.
427	
428	### Threat model — what this is NOT
429	
430	- **Not a sandbox.** The verifier still runs as your user. A malicious *builder*-side prompt that gets the **builder** to run `rm -rf` is unaffected by any of this — that's the builder's permission model, not the verifier's. The verifier's job is to never *itself* be the source of mutation.
431	- **Don't load untrusted personas.** Layers 1 and 2 are configured by the persona file. A persona you don't trust can declare a different `allowed_script` or omit `bash_policy` entirely. Pin your personas the same way you'd pin any other config that controls subprocess execution.
432	
433	## Known limitations (v1)
434	
435	- **One domain ships:** SQLite. Other domains follow the pattern above but aren't included. A stub `.pi/verifier/agents/verifier.md` is present as a non-functional placeholder.
436	- **Multi-verifier fan-out is not supported.** One verifier per builder, enforced server-side (a second connection on the same socket gets a `bye {reason: "duplicate connection"}` and is dropped).
437	- **Late-attach across processes is not supported.** Use `/verify` from the same builder Pi to spawn its own verifier; you can't `/attach <id>` to a builder running in another shell.
438	- **Windows-native is untested.** Use WSL.
439	- **The new-OS-window dispatch covers Ghostty / iTerm / Terminal.app / WezTerm / gnome-terminal / konsole / kitty / alacritty / xterm.** Other emulators fall through to a `tmux attach -t verifier-<sid>` instruction printed to stderr; the detached tmux session is the source of truth so you can attach manually.
440	- **Domain selection via `--verifier-agent <name>`.** Defaults to `verify_sqlite`. The flag value is the bare persona name (no `.md`, no path) and is resolved under `.pi/verifier/agents/`. Only the SQLite persona ships with v1, but you can author and select a sibling persona without editing source.
441	- **The verifier's persona body is rendered into `--system-prompt` as a full overwrite.** Pi's default system prompt is replaced, not appended to — by design. Don't expect Pi's standard "coding agent" affordances to be available in the verifier.
442
