1	/**
2	 * Tmux + new-OS-window launcher for the Pi Verifier Agent (`$TMUX`-aware).
3	 *
4	 * Single shared implementation for both `--verifiable` auto-spawn and the
5	 * `/verify` slash command. Idempotent: a second call when the verifier is
6	 * already running is a no-op + return, never a duplicate spawn.
7	 *
8	 * Two branches, intentionally:
9	 *
10	 *   1. IN-TMUX BRANCH (`$TMUX` set) — the builder is already running inside
11	 *      a tmux session. We add the verifier as a *sibling window* in that
12	 *      same session.
13	 *
14	 *      Primary reason this branch exists: `/drive` (the tmux-based E2E
15	 *      harness) can only observe panes/windows in tmux sessions it owns.
16	 *      Without this branch, the launcher would spin up a *separate* tmux
17	 *      session that drive cannot reach, breaking end-to-end validation.
18	 *      Three callers benefit, in order of importance:
19	 *        (1) /drive E2E test                        [primary motivation]
20	 *        (2) CI / tmux-based automation              [same plumbing]
21	 *        (3) tmux power users running pi day-to-day  [incidental win]
22	 *
23	 *   2. NEW-OS-WINDOW BRANCH (`$TMUX` unset) — normal native-terminal user
24	 *      (Ghostty / iTerm / Terminal.app / Wezterm / gnome-terminal / etc.).
25	 *      The user wants two visible terminal windows. The detached tmux
26	 *      session is the source of truth (survives window close, can be
27	 *      re-attached); the OS window is just an attached client.
28	 *
29	 * The persona system prompt is rendered HERE, before spawn — frontmatter
30	 * vars (BUILDER_SESSION_ID, SOCKET_PATH, etc.) are substituted into the
31	 * persona body and passed to the verifier child via `--system-prompt`.
32	 */
33	
34	import { execFile } from "node:child_process";
35	import { promises as fs } from "node:fs";
36	import * as os from "node:os";
37	import * as path from "node:path";
38	import { promisify } from "node:util";
39	
40	import { parseVerifierPersona, templateBody } from "./frontmatter.js";
41	import { ensureSocketDir, resolveSocketPath, writeSocketRef } from "./socket-path.js";
42	
43	const execFileP = promisify(execFile);
44	
45	// ─── Public types ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
46	
47	export interface SpawnOpts {
48	  /** `ctx.sessionManager.getSessionId()` — the canonical session id. */
49	  sessionId: string;
50	  /** Absolute path to `.pi/verifier/agents/verify_<domain>.md`. */
51	  agentPath: string;
52	  /** Absolute path to repo root, used to resolve `apps/verifier/verifier.ts`. */
53	  runtimeRoot: string;
54	  /** `ctx.cwd` — used for `.pi/state/` breadcrumb resolution. */
55	  cwd: string;
56	  /** `.pi/settings.json` — only `verifier.terminalCommand` is consulted. */
57	  settings?: { verifier?: { terminalCommand?: string } };
58	  /** Absolute path to `~/.pi/agent/sessions/<sid>.jsonl` — fed into `<BUILDER_SESSION_FILE>`. */
59	  builderSessionFile: string;
60	}
61	
62	export type SpawnMode = "in-tmux" | "new-window";
63	
64	export interface SpawnResult {
65	  tmuxSession: string;
66	  mode: SpawnMode;
67	  /** Auto-generated bash wrapper that exports env + runs the verifier pi child. */
68	  wrapperPath: string;
69	  /**
70	   * File the wrapper redirects pi's stderr into (mirrored to the terminal
71	   * via `tee` so the tmux pane still shows it). Read on spawn-failure to
72	   * surface pi's actual error in the builder — far more useful than the
73	   * generic "verifier didn't connect in time" timeout.
74	   */
75	  stderrLogPath: string;
76	}
77	
78	// ─── spawnVerifierChild ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
79	
80	/**
81	 * Spawn (or re-attach to) the verifier child for `opts.sessionId`.
82	 *
83	 * Idempotent: if a tmux session/window with the expected name already
84	 * exists, returns early without spawning a duplicate.
85	 */
86	export async function spawnVerifierChild(opts: SpawnOpts): Promise<SpawnResult> {
87	  const tmuxSession = `verifier-${opts.sessionId}`;
88	
89	  // Resolve socket paths up-front — we need SOCKET_PATH for system-prompt
90	  // templating, and the breadcrumb so the verifier child can find the
91	  // socket by --builder-session alone.
92	  const { socketPath, refPath } = resolveSocketPath(opts.sessionId, opts.cwd);
93	  await ensureSocketDir();
94	  await writeSocketRef(socketPath, refPath);
95	
96	  // ─── Render the persona system prompt before spawn ───────────────────
97	  const personaContent = await fs.readFile(opts.agentPath, "utf8");
98	  const { frontmatter, body } = parseVerifierPersona(personaContent);
99	
100	  const rendered = templateBody(body, {
101	    BUILDER_SESSION_ID: opts.sessionId,
102	    BUILDER_SESSION_FILE: opts.builderSessionFile,
103	    DOMAIN: frontmatter.domain,
104	    MAX_LOOPS: String(frontmatter.max_loops ?? 3),
105	    SOCKET_PATH: socketPath,
106	  });
107	
108	  // Stash the rendered prompt in a tempfile so it's inspectable post-mortem
109	  // AND so the wrapper script can load it via `$(cat ...)` instead of having
110	  // it embedded in the tmux command line. macOS ARG_MAX (~256KB for argv +
111	  // envp combined) is easily blown by a 10KB system prompt + ~50 -e KEY=VAL
112	  // env flags inline — embedding the prompt in a file keeps tmux's command
113	  // line short.
114	  const systemPromptFile = path.join(os.tmpdir(), `pi-verifier-${opts.sessionId}.system.md`);
115	  await fs.writeFile(systemPromptFile, rendered, { encoding: "utf8", mode: 0o600 });
116	
117	  // ─── Build the spawn wrapper ─────────────────────────────────────────
118	  // Instead of passing all the env via tmux `-e` flags AND the system prompt
119	  // inline AND the long pi command — all of which combine to blow ARG_MAX
120	  // on macOS — we write a tiny wrapper shell script that exports the env
121	  // and exec's pi. tmux then just runs `bash <wrapper>`. Wrapper file size
122	  // doesn't count toward exec()'s ARG_MAX; only the tmux command's argv does.
123	  //
124	  // Pi defaults to its full tool set; we forward only what the persona's
125	  // `tools:` field declares (architectural read-only guarantee).
126	  const verifierEntry = path.join(opts.runtimeRoot, "apps", "verifier", "verifier.ts");
127	  const wrapperPath = path.join(os.tmpdir(), `pi-verifier-${opts.sessionId}.spawn.sh`);
128	  const stderrLogPath = path.join(os.tmpdir(), `pi-verifier-${opts.sessionId}.stderr.log`);
129	  const wrapperContent = buildSpawnWrapper({
130	    env: process.env,
131	    systemPromptFile,
132	    verifierEntry,
133	    sessionId: opts.sessionId,
134	    agentPath: opts.agentPath,
135	    tools: normalizeToolsList(frontmatter.tools),
136	    model: frontmatter.model,
137	    stderrLogPath,
138	  });
139	  await fs.writeFile(wrapperPath, wrapperContent, { encoding: "utf8", mode: 0o700 });
140	
141	  // ─── Idempotency check ───────────────────────────────────────────────
142	  if (await verifierAlreadyRunning(tmuxSession)) {
143	    return {
144	      tmuxSession,
145	      mode: process.env.TMUX ? "in-tmux" : "new-window",
146	      wrapperPath,
147	      stderrLogPath,
148	    };
149	  }
150	
151	  // The actual command tmux runs is a single short string: `bash <wrapper>`.
152	  // Env exports + system-prompt-from-file happen inside the wrapper, so
153	  // tmux's own argv stays well under ARG_MAX regardless of how chunky the
154	  // calling process's env or the rendered persona is.
155	  const verifierCommand = `bash ${shellSingleQuote(wrapperPath)}`;
156	
157	  // ─── Branch on $TMUX ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
158	  if (process.env.TMUX) {
159	    // ── IN-TMUX BRANCH ──────────────────────────────────────────────
160	    // This branch primarily exists so /drive can validate the system
161	    // end-to-end (drive is tmux-based and can only observe panes in
162	    // tmux sessions it owns); also incidentally helps users who live
163	    // in tmux daily. Three callers benefit:
164	    //   (1) /drive E2E test                       [primary]
165	    //   (2) CI / tmux-based automation
166	    //   (3) tmux power users                      [incidental]
167	    // We create the verifier as a sibling window in the existing tmux
168	    // session — same parent tmux process, same observability surface.
169	    // `-c <cwd>` makes the new window inherit the builder's cwd.
170	    // Env propagates via the wrapper script, NOT tmux `-e` flags
171	    // (those would re-introduce the ARG_MAX blowup we just avoided).
172	    await execFileP("tmux", [
173	      "new-window",
174	      "-n", tmuxSession,
175	      "-c", opts.cwd,
176	      verifierCommand,
177	    ]);
178	    return { tmuxSession, mode: "in-tmux", wrapperPath, stderrLogPath };
179	  }
180	
181	  // ── NEW-OS-WINDOW BRANCH ───────────────────────────────────────────
182	  // Native terminal — user wants two visible terminal windows. Detached
183	  // tmux is the source of truth (survives window close, re-attachable
184	  // by sessionId); the OS window is just an attached client.
185	  // `-c <cwd>` and `-e KEY=VAL ...` mirror the in-tmux branch above:
186	  // verifier inherits builder's cwd and env.
187	  await execFileP("tmux", [
188	    "new-session",
189	    "-d",
190	    "-s", tmuxSession,
191	    "-c", opts.cwd,
192	    verifierCommand,
193	  ]);
194	  // Apply verifier-friendly tmux options scoped to THIS session only.
195	  // The in-tmux branch above leaves the user's existing session config
196	  // untouched on purpose; only sessions we create get our defaults.
197	  await applyVerifierTmuxOptions(tmuxSession);
198	  await openOsWindowAttachedTo(tmuxSession, opts.settings);
199	  return { tmuxSession, mode: "new-window", wrapperPath, stderrLogPath };
200	}
201	
202	/**
203	 * Build a wrapper shell script that exports the calling process's env (minus
204	 * a small skip list) and exec's pi as the verifier child.
205	 *
206	 * Why a wrapper instead of `tmux -e KEY=VAL ...`:
207	 *   macOS's `exec*()` syscalls enforce ARG_MAX (~256KB combined argv + envp).
208	 *   With ~50 env vars (some kilobytes long like PATH and API keys) AND the
209	 *   ~10KB rendered system prompt embedded inline, the tmux command line
210	 *   easily blows ARG_MAX. The wrapper sidesteps it: file size doesn't count
211	 *   toward exec()'s argv limit, only the live argv passed to tmux does.
212	 *
213	 *   Tmux's command becomes simply `bash <wrapper>`. All the bulk lives in
214	 *   the file — env exports, system-prompt-from-tempfile, the pi invocation.
215	 *
216	 * Why every env var, not a curated subset: the verifier behaves exactly like
217	 * the builder for LLM/tool resolution. Any API key, locale, PATH addition,
218	 * or feature flag the user sets at the shell level needs to reach the
219	 * verifier. Filtering risks silently dropping something the verifier needs.
220	 *
221	 * Excluded keys: process-tied (`_`, `OLDPWD`, `PWD` — `-c` covers cwd) and
222	 * `TMUX*` (so the new session doesn't think it's nested in the parent tmux).
223	 */
224	interface BuildSpawnWrapperOpts {
225	  env: NodeJS.ProcessEnv;
226	  systemPromptFile: string;
227	  verifierEntry: string;
228	  sessionId: string;
229	  agentPath: string;
230	  /** Comma-separated tool list. Empty / `"*"` → omit `--tools` (pi defaults). */
231	  tools: string;
232	  /**
233	   * Persona's `model:` frontmatter value, passed to pi via `--model` so the
234	   * verifier child uses the persona-declared model regardless of what the
235	   * user's pi config has selected globally. Without this, a user running
236	   * deepseek-v4-pro as their default would get a deepseek verifier even when
237	   * the persona declares anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6.
238	   */
239	  model: string;
240	  /**
241	   * File to capture pi's stderr into. The wrapper redirects stderr through
242	   * `tee`, so the file gets pi's actual error output (e.g. "model not
243	   * found: moonshot/kimi-k2.6") AND the tmux pane still shows it. The
244	   * builder reads this file when the spawn-hello timeout fires so the
245	   * surfaced system message names the real cause instead of just "didn't
246	   * connect in time."
247	   */
248	  stderrLogPath: string;
249	}
250	
251	function buildSpawnWrapper(opts: BuildSpawnWrapperOpts): string {
252	  const skip = new Set(["_", "OLDPWD", "PWD"]);
253	  const exports: string[] = [];
254	  for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(opts.env)) {
255	    if (v === undefined) continue;
256	    if (skip.has(k)) continue;
257	    if (k.startsWith("TMUX")) continue; // don't leak parent tmux state
258	    // Skip identifiers shells can't validly export (e.g. with `(` or `=`).
259	    if (!/^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$/.test(k)) continue;
260	    exports.push(`export ${k}=${shellSingleQuote(v)}`);
261	  }
262	
263	  const piArgs = [
264	    `-e ${shellSingleQuote(opts.verifierEntry)}`,
265	    "--child",
266	    `--builder-session ${shellSingleQuote(opts.sessionId)}`,
267	    `--agent ${shellSingleQuote(opts.agentPath)}`,
268	    `--system-prompt "$(cat ${shellSingleQuote(opts.systemPromptFile)})"`,
269	    `--model ${shellSingleQuote(opts.model)}`,
270	  ];
271	  if (opts.tools && opts.tools !== "*") {
272	    piArgs.push(`--tools ${shellSingleQuote(opts.tools)}`);
273	  }
274	
275	  // Notes on the wrapper shape:
276	  //
277	  // - We deliberately do NOT use `set -e` and do NOT `exec` pi: we need
278	  //   lines past the `pi` invocation to run on a non-zero exit so we can
279	  //   record pi's exit code into the stderr log. With `set -e` + `exec`,
280	  //   the wrapper would die mid-pipeline and the builder's diagnosis
281	  //   would only ever see whatever pi flushed before the kill.
282	  //
283	  // - Stderr is redirected through `tee -a "$STDERR_LOG" >&2` (bash
284	  //   process substitution). That writes pi's stderr to the log file
285	  //   AND mirrors it back to fd 2, so anyone attached to the tmux pane
286	  //   still sees the error in real time. Stdout is left alone because
287	  //   pi's interactive TUI uses the terminal directly (ioctl on
288	  //   /dev/tty), and tee'ing stdout would mangle ANSI escape sequences.
289	  //
290	  // - Truncate the log on each spawn (`: > "$STDERR_LOG"`) so the
291	  //   builder doesn't surface a stale error from a previous run.
292	  return [
293	    "#!/usr/bin/env bash",
294	    "# Auto-generated by Pi Verifier launcher.ts.",
295	    "# Sets up env, runs the verifier pi child, captures stderr to a log.",
296	    "# Wrapped in a script so the tmux command line stays tiny (avoids",
297	    "# ARG_MAX on macOS with verbose env).",
298	    "",
299	    `STDERR_LOG=${shellSingleQuote(opts.stderrLogPath)}`,
300	    `: > "$STDERR_LOG"`,
301	    "",
302	    "# ─── Env (forwarded from the builder process) ────────────────────────",
303	    ...exports,
304	    "",
305	    "# ─── Run the verifier (capture stderr; mirror to terminal) ───────────",
306	    // Every piArg line gets a `\` continuation so the `2> >(tee ...)`
307	    // redirect on the next line attaches to THIS pi invocation rather
308	    // than starting a separate command. Without the continuation on the
309	    // last arg, bash would parse the redirect as its own statement and
310	    // the stderr capture would silently miss pi's actual output.
311	    "pi \\",
312	    ...piArgs.map((a) => `  ${a} \\`),
313	    `  2> >(tee -a "$STDERR_LOG" >&2)`,
314	    "",
315	    "EXIT_CODE=$?",
316	    `echo "" >> "$STDERR_LOG"`,
317	    `echo "[wrapper] pi exited with code $EXIT_CODE" >> "$STDERR_LOG"`,
318	    "exit $EXIT_CODE",
319	    "",
320	  ].join("\n");
321	}
322	
323	/**
324	 * Apply verifier-friendly tmux options to a session WE just created.
325	 *
326	 * These are session-scoped — they don't leak into the user's other tmux
327	 * sessions. Each set-option call is best-effort; older tmux versions or
328	 * unrecognized options shouldn't block the spawn.
329	 *
330	 * Defaults chosen for engineer ergonomics:
331	 *   - mouse on:          scroll wheel scrolls scrollback, click selects panes.
332	 *   - status off:        hide tmux's bottom green status bar — the verifier's
333	 *                        own status chip already shows connection state, so
334	 *                        the tmux bar is just visual noise (and steals a row).
335	 *   - history-limit:     10000 lines instead of tmux's default 2000 — useful
336	 *                        when scrolling back across multiple verification cycles.
337	 *
338	 * Power users can override by setting `verifier.terminalCommand` in
339	 * `.pi/settings.json` to a template that pipes through their own tmux config,
340	 * or by editing this list.
341	 */
342	async function applyVerifierTmuxOptions(tmuxSession: string): Promise<void> {
343	  // Defaults chosen for engineer ergonomics:
344	  //   - mouse on:           scroll wheel + click-to-focus
345	  //   - status off:         hide the bottom green status bar (the verifier's
346	  //                         own footer + status bar already convey state)
347	  //   - history-limit:      10k lines (tmux default 2000 runs out fast)
348	  //   - set-clipboard on:   pushes mouse selections to the OS clipboard via
349	  //                         OSC52. Modern macOS terminals (iTerm, Ghostty,
350	  //                         Terminal.app, WezTerm) all support OSC52, so a
351	  //                         normal mouse-drag-to-select inside the verifier
352	  //                         pane Just Works for copy-paste — no need to
353	  //                         enter tmux copy-mode. Hold Option (macOS) /
354	  //                         Shift (some emulators) while dragging if you
355	  //                         want to bypass tmux mouse mode entirely for a
356	  //                         given selection (purely native terminal select).
357	  const opts: Array<[string, string]> = [
358	    ["mouse", "on"],
359	    ["status", "off"],
360	    ["history-limit", "10000"],
361	    ["set-clipboard", "on"],
362	  ];
363	  for (const [name, value] of opts) {
364	    try {
365	      await execFileP("tmux", ["set-option", "-t", tmuxSession, name, value]);
366	    } catch {
367	      // Non-fatal — older tmux may not recognize an option, or the
368	      // session might already be torn down. Don't block the spawn.
369	    }
370	  }
371	}
372	
373	// ─── killVerifierChild ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
374	
375	/**
376	 * Best-effort teardown. Swallows "session/window not found" errors so it's
377	 * safe to call from `session_shutdown` regardless of whether the verifier
378	 * was ever spawned.
379	 */
380	export async function killVerifierChild(sessionId: string): Promise<void> {
381	  const tmuxSession = `verifier-${sessionId}`;
382	  if (process.env.TMUX) {
383	    // In-tmux mode: kill just the sibling window. The parent tmux session
384	    // (the one the user is in) keeps running.
385	    await tmuxSwallowMissing(["kill-window", "-t", tmuxSession]);
386	    return;
387	  }
388	  // New-OS-window mode: the entire detached session is ours to destroy.
389	  await tmuxSwallowMissing(["kill-session", "-t", tmuxSession]);
390	}
391	
392	// ─── Verifier command construction ───────────────────────────────────────────
393	//
394	// (Previously a `buildVerifierCommand` helper inlined the pi invocation.
395	// Replaced by `buildSpawnWrapper` above — the wrapper-script approach keeps
396	// the tmux argv tiny, sidestepping macOS ARG_MAX. The command tmux runs is
397	// just `bash <wrapperPath>`; everything else lives inside the wrapper.)
398	
399	/**
400	 * Normalize the persona's `tools:` frontmatter field into a comma-separated
401	 * string with no whitespace (matches Pi's `--tools` flag format), and ALWAYS
402	 * append `verifier_prompt` — that tool is registered by `verifier.ts` and is
403	 * the system-required transport for sending corrective feedback back to the
404	 * builder. Persona authors shouldn't have to remember to list it; if it's
405	 * missing from `--tools`, pi filters it out and the LLM sees "tool not
406	 * found" when the persona's body tells it to call `verifier_prompt`.
407	 *
408	 *   "read, grep, find, ls, bash"  →  "read,grep,find,ls,bash,verifier_prompt"
409	 *   "read"                        →  "read,verifier_prompt"
410	 *   ""                            →  "" (caller skips --tools entirely;
411	 *                                        pi defaults include the extension's
412	 *                                        tools, so verifier_prompt is visible)
413	 */
414	function normalizeToolsList(toolsField: string): string {
415	  const tools = toolsField
416	    .split(",")
417	    .map((t) => t.trim())
418	    .filter((t) => t.length > 0);
419	  if (tools.length === 0) return "";
420	  if (!tools.includes("verifier_prompt")) tools.push("verifier_prompt");
421	  return tools.join(",");
422	}
423	
424	/**
425	 * POSIX single-quote shell escaping. Single-quote runs are literal in sh,
426	 * so we close, emit an escaped quote (`'\''`), and re-open. Result is a
427	 * single quoted token that round-trips any byte sequence except NUL.
428	 */
429	function shellSingleQuote(value: string): string {
430	  return `'${value.replace(/'/g, "'\\''")}'`;
431	}
432	
433	// ─── Idempotency helpers ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
434	
435	/**
436	 * Detect whether a verifier with this session name is already running.
437	 *
438	 * In-tmux mode: list windows in the current session; match on name.
439	 * Out-of-tmux mode: ask tmux whether a session by that name exists.
440	 *
441	 * Both forms swallow "no server" / "no such session" — those just mean
442	 * "not running yet", which is the happy-path spawn case.
443	 */
444	async function verifierAlreadyRunning(tmuxSession: string): Promise<boolean> {
445	  if (process.env.TMUX) {
446	    try {
447	      const { stdout } = await execFileP("tmux", ["list-windows", "-F", "#{window_name}"]);
448	      const names = stdout.split("\n").map((s) => s.trim()).filter(Boolean);
449	      return names.includes(tmuxSession);
450	    } catch {
451	      // No tmux server / not in a session we can list — treat as "not running".
452	      return false;
453	    }
454	  }
455	  try {
456	    await execFileP("tmux", ["has-session", "-t", tmuxSession]);
457	    return true;
458	  } catch {
459	    return false;
460	  }
461	}
462	
463	async function tmuxSwallowMissing(args: string[]): Promise<void> {
464	  try {
465	    await execFileP("tmux", args);
466	  } catch (err) {
467	    const stderr = ((err as { stderr?: string }).stderr ?? "").toLowerCase();
468	    if (
469	      stderr.includes("can't find") ||
470	      stderr.includes("no such") ||
471	      stderr.includes("session not found") ||
472	      stderr.includes("window not found") ||
473	      stderr.includes("no server running")
474	    ) {
475	      return;
476	    }
477	    throw err;
478	  }
479	}
480	
481	// ─── OS-window dispatch (new-OS-window branch only) ──────────────────────────
482	
483	/**
484	 * Open a visible OS-level terminal window attached to the given tmux session.
485	 *
486	 * Order of preference:
487	 *   1. settings.verifier.terminalCommand (template; `{cmd}` ← `tmux attach -t <session>`)
488	 *   2. macOS auto-detection by $TERM_PROGRAM
489	 *   3. Linux: $TERMINAL, then known emulators in PATH
490	 *   4. Fallback: print the manual `tmux attach` instruction (don't error)
491	 */
492	async function openOsWindowAttachedTo(
493	  tmuxSession: string,
494	  settings: SpawnOpts["settings"],
495	): Promise<void> {
496	  const attachCmd = `tmux attach -t ${tmuxSession}`;
497	
498	  // 1. Settings override wins over auto-detection.
499	  const override = settings?.verifier?.terminalCommand;
500	  if (override && override.length > 0) {
501	    const expanded = override.replace(/\{cmd\}/g, attachCmd);
502	    // Run via `sh -c` so the user's template can use full shell syntax
503	    // (pipes, redirects, env-var expansion). This is the explicit escape
504	    // hatch — auto-detection tries to use `execFile` everywhere else.
505	    await execFileP("sh", ["-c", expanded]);
506	    return;
507	  }
508	
509	  // 2. macOS dispatch.
510	  //
511	  // Strategy: try the user's $TERM_PROGRAM first (best UX when it works), then
512	  // ALWAYS fall through to Terminal.app via osascript. Terminal.app is
513	  // preinstalled on every macOS and `do script` reliably opens a visible
514	  // window — that's our "engineers can see this" guarantee.
515	  //
516	  // The per-emulator fast paths (Ghostty, WezTerm, etc.) are wrapped in
517	  // try/catch because their CLI args/behavior vary across versions; if they
518	  // throw OR if $TERM_PROGRAM is unknown (vscode, WarpTerminal, Hyper, …),
519	  // we fall through to Terminal.app. Power users who want their native
520	  // emulator can set `verifier.terminalCommand` in .pi/settings.json.
521	  if (process.platform === "darwin") {
522	    const term = process.env.TERM_PROGRAM;
523	    if (term && (await tryDispatchMacOS(term, attachCmd, tmuxSession))) {
524	      return;
525	    }
526	    // Universal fallback: Terminal.app via osascript. Always opens a visible
527	    // window so the verifier never runs headless.
528	    if (await tryOpenTerminalApp(attachCmd)) {
529	      return;
530	    }
531	    fallbackInstruction(tmuxSession);
532	    return;
533	  }
534	
535	  // 3. Linux: $TERMINAL, then known emulators.
536	  if (process.platform === "linux") {
537	    const explicit = process.env.TERMINAL;
538	    if (explicit && (await commandExists(explicit))) {
539	      await spawnLinuxEmulator(explicit, attachCmd, tmuxSession);
540	      return;
541	    }
542	    for (const candidate of ["gnome-terminal", "konsole", "kitty", "alacritty", "xterm"]) {
543	      if (await commandExists(candidate)) {
544	        await spawnLinuxEmulator(candidate, attachCmd, tmuxSession);
545	        return;
546	      }
547	    }
548	    fallbackInstruction(tmuxSession);
549	    return;
550	  }
551	
552	  // 4. Other platforms — no auto-detection, just print the instruction.
553	  fallbackInstruction(tmuxSession);
554	}
555	
556	/**
557	 * Per-emulator argv shape on Linux. `gnome-terminal` and `konsole` use
558	 * `-e`/`--` conventions that are not universal — kitty/alacritty/xterm
559	 * accept the command after a literal `-e`.
560	 */
561	async function spawnLinuxEmulator(
562	  emulator: string,
563	  attachCmd: string,
564	  tmuxSession: string,
565	): Promise<void> {
566	  switch (path.basename(emulator)) {
567	    case "gnome-terminal":
568	      await execFileP(emulator, ["--", "tmux", "attach", "-t", tmuxSession]);
569	      return;
570	    case "konsole":
571	      await execFileP(emulator, ["-e", "tmux", "attach", "-t", tmuxSession]);
572	      return;
573	    case "kitty":
574	    case "alacritty":
575	    case "xterm":
576	      await execFileP(emulator, ["-e", "tmux", "attach", "-t", tmuxSession]);
577	      return;
578	    default:
579	      // Unknown $TERMINAL — assume it accepts `-e <cmd>` like xterm.
580	      await execFileP(emulator, ["-e", attachCmd]);
581	      return;
582	  }
583	}
584	
585	/**
586	 * `which`-style lookup. Returns true iff `command` resolves to an
587	 * executable on the user's PATH.
588	 */
589	async function commandExists(command: string): Promise<boolean> {
590	  try {
591	    await execFileP("sh", ["-c", `command -v ${shellSingleQuote(command)}`]);
592	    return true;
593	  } catch {
594	    return false;
595	  }
596	}
597	
598	/**
599	 * Last-resort: emit a manual-attach instruction. Don't throw — the
600	 * detached tmux session is already running and usable; we just couldn't
601	 * pop a window for the user.
602	 */
603	function fallbackInstruction(tmuxSession: string): void {
604	  process.stderr.write(
605	    `Verifier started in detached tmux session. Attach with: tmux attach -t ${tmuxSession}\n`,
606	  );
607	}
608	
609	/**
610	 * Try to dispatch a new visible window for the user's detected $TERM_PROGRAM.
611	 * Each branch is wrapped in try/catch — if any throws (CLI flag mismatch, app
612	 * not installed, etc.), we return false so the caller falls through to the
613	 * Terminal.app universal fallback.
614	 *
615	 * Returns true if dispatch succeeded (no throw), false otherwise. Note: a
616	 * `true` return only means the spawned command exited 0; some emulators
617	 * (notably `open -na` against Ghostty) may exit 0 without actually opening a
618	 * window. That's documented in the SpawnOpts.settings.verifier.terminalCommand
619	 * escape hatch — set it explicitly if auto-detect doesn't open a window for
620	 * your emulator.
621	 */
622	async function tryDispatchMacOS(
623	  term: string,
624	  attachCmd: string,
625	  tmuxSession: string,
626	): Promise<boolean> {
627	  try {
628	    switch (term) {
629	      case "Apple_Terminal":
630	        await execFileP("osascript", [
631	          "-e",
632	          `tell application "Terminal"
633	             activate
634	             do script "${attachCmd}"
635	           end tell`,
636	        ]);
637	        return true;
638	      case "iTerm.app":
639	        await execFileP("osascript", [
640	          "-e",
641	          `tell application "iTerm"
642	             activate
643	             create window with default profile
644	             tell current session of current window to write text "${attachCmd}"
645	           end tell`,
646	        ]);
647	        return true;
648	      case "ghostty":
649	      case "Ghostty":
650	        // Prefer the `ghostty` CLI binary if available — most reliable across
651	        // versions. Falls back to `open -na` against the app bundle, which
652	        // works for some Ghostty builds and not others (caller falls through
653	        // to Terminal.app on failure either way).
654	        if (await commandExists("ghostty")) {
655	          await execFileP("ghostty", ["-e", attachCmd]);
656	        } else {
657	          await execFileP("open", ["-na", "Ghostty", "--args", "-e", attachCmd]);
658	        }
659	        return true;
660	      case "WezTerm":
661	        await execFileP("wezterm", [
662	          "cli",
663	          "spawn",
664	          "--new-window",
665	          "--",
666	          "tmux",
667	          "attach",
668	          "-t",
669	          tmuxSession,
670	        ]);
671	        return true;
672	      default:
673	        // Unknown $TERM_PROGRAM (vscode, WarpTerminal, Hyper, Tabby, …).
674	        // Don't try anything fancy — caller falls through to Terminal.app.
675	        return false;
676	    }
677	  } catch {
678	    return false;
679	  }
680	}
681	
682	/**
683	 * Universal macOS fallback: open a Terminal.app window via AppleScript and
684	 * run the tmux attach command in it. Always works because Terminal.app is
685	 * preinstalled and `do script` is a stable AppleScript verb.
686	 *
687	 * Returns true on success. Caller falls through to printed instruction
688	 * only if even this fails (extremely unlikely on a working macOS).
689	 */
690	async function tryOpenTerminalApp(attachCmd: string): Promise<boolean> {
691	  try {
692	    await execFileP("osascript", [
693	      "-e",
694	      `tell application "Terminal"
695	         activate
696	         do script "${attachCmd}"
697	       end tell`,
698	    ]);
699	    return true;
700	  } catch {
701	    return false;
702	  }
703	}

4	
5	# Install Pi Verifier Agent
6	
7	## Purpose
8	
9	Set up the Pi Verifier Agent for development on a fresh clone. Walks the user through every check the system needs — runtime tools (node / python / uv / tmux / sqlite3 / pi), TypeScript dependencies, the verifier persona + script, and an LLM provider API key — without ever starting an interactive Pi session. Interactive: ask the user when a choice is needed (e.g., which API key to set), install what can be installed automatically.
10	
11	## Variables
12	
13	SOURCE_REPO: The repo root this command runs from
14	APP_DIR: `apps/verifier/`
15	PERSONA: `.pi/verifier/agents/verify_sqlite.md`
16	SCRIPT: `.pi/verifier/scripts/verify_sqlite.py`
17	PROMPT_TEMPLATE: `.pi/verifier/prompts/verify_on_stop.md`
18	SETTINGS: `.pi/settings.json`
19	DEFAULT_MODEL: `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6` (per `verify_sqlite.md` frontmatter)
20	
21	## Codebase Structure
22	
23	```
24	the-verifier-agent/
25	├── apps/verifier/                  # TypeScript extensions (verifiable.ts + verifier.ts + _shared/)
26	│   ├── package.json                # post-A1: workspace lives here, not at root
27	│   └── tsconfig.json
28	├── .pi/
29	│   ├── settings.json               # { skills, sessionDir }
30	│   └── verifier/
31	│       ├── agents/verify_sqlite.md # persona — frontmatter declares model, max_loops, bash_policy
32	│       ├── prompts/                # verify_on_stop.md, builder_error.md
33	│       └── scripts/verify_sqlite.py# astral-uv read-only SQLite wrapper (the only allowed bash cmd)
34	├── justfile                        # default | verifier | sqlite | image | python | prime | clean
35	└── .env                            # NOT in repo; user creates with provider API keys
36	```
37	
38	## Instructions
39	
40	- Run every check via Bash — do not assume anything is installed.
41	- Show a one-line pass/fail status after each check.
42	- Critical deps (`node`, `pi`, `tmux`) gate the install — stop and instruct the user if missing.
43	- For optional deps (`drive`, `WezTerm`, etc.) note absence but continue.
44	- For the API key step: confirm a provider key is set in either `process.env` or `.env`. **Never read or print key values** — only confirm presence.
45	- Do NOT start `pi`, do NOT run any `just v*` recipe, do NOT open windows — this command verifies readiness only.
46	- If a `.env` doesn't exist, offer to create one with the chosen provider's key as a placeholder (commented), but never write a real key.
47	
48	## Workflow
49	
50	### Step 1 — Critical prerequisites (gate)
51	
52	If any of these are missing, stop and instruct the user before continuing.
53	
54	1. Check `node`: `command -v node && node --version`. Need ≥ 20. If missing → `brew install node` (macOS) or use a Node version manager (nvm, fnm, volta).
55	2. Check `pi`: `command -v pi && pi --version`. The Pi Coding Agent CLI. If missing → `npm install -g @mariozechner/pi-coding-agent` (or the user's preferred install path; consult [Pi Coding Agent docs](https://github.com/mariozechner/pi-coding-agent)).
56	3. Check `tmux`: `command -v tmux && tmux -V`. Need 3.x+. If missing → `brew install tmux` (macOS) or `apt install tmux` (Debian/Ubuntu).
57	
58	Stop and report each missing critical dep separately so the user can install incrementally.
59	
60	### Step 2 — Standard prerequisites
61	
62	These are all required by the verifier script or the `just` recipes; install missing ones via the listed commands.
63	
64	4. Check `uv` (astral-uv — runs the SQLite verifier script with inline PEP 723 deps):
65	   `command -v uv && uv --version`. If missing → `curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh`.
66	5. Check `python3` (the verifier script's shebang resolves to `uv run --script` which uses Python ≥ 3.11):
67	   `command -v python3 && python3 --version`.
68	6. Check `sqlite3`: `command -v sqlite3 && sqlite3 --version`. Used internally by the verifier script for dot-commands like `.schema`.
69	7. Check `just`: `command -v just && just --version`. Optional but every workflow command in the README runs through justfile recipes — strongly recommended. If missing → `brew install just` (macOS) or [installation instructions](https://github.com/casey/just#installation).
70	
71	### Step 3 — Optional environment notes
72	
73	8. Detect terminal emulator: `echo "$TERM_PROGRAM"`. The launcher's per-emulator dispatch knows about Ghostty, iTerm, Apple_Terminal, WezTerm. If `$TERM_PROGRAM` is something else (e.g., `vscode`, `WarpTerminal`), the launcher falls back to a Terminal.app window via `osascript` — also fine.
74	
75	### Step 4 — Install TypeScript dependencies
76	
77	10. Run `cd apps/verifier && npm install`. This installs `@mariozechner/pi-coding-agent`, `@mariozechner/pi-tui`, `typebox`, `typescript`, `@types/node` into `apps/verifier/node_modules/`.
78	
79	### Step 5 — Verify configuration files
80	
81	11. Persona file exists and frontmatter is parseable:
82	    - `[ -f .pi/verifier/agents/verify_sqlite.md ] && echo persona-present`
83	    - The frontmatter must declare `name`, `description`, `tools`, `model`, `domain`, `bash_policy.{mode, allowed_script, runner}`, optionally `max_loops`. The exact contract is enforced at runtime by `apps/verifier/_shared/frontmatter.ts:parseVerifierPersona`.
84	12. Script file exists and is executable:
85	    - `[ -f .pi/verifier/scripts/verify_sqlite.py ] && [ -x .pi/verifier/scripts/verify_sqlite.py ] && echo script-executable`
86	    - If not executable: `chmod +x .pi/verifier/scripts/verify_sqlite.py`.
87	13. User-prompt template exists:
88	    - `[ -f .pi/verifier/prompts/verify_on_stop.md ] && echo prompt-template-present`
89	14. Project settings exist:
90	    - `[ -f .pi/settings.json ] && python3 -c 'import json; json.load(open(".pi/settings.json"))' && echo settings-valid-json`
91	
92	### Step 6 — Verify environment / provider API key
93	
94	15. Default model across all verifier personas is `openai/gpt-5.5` → the canonical key is `OPENAI_API_KEY`. Check it without printing the value:
95	    - `[ -n "${OPENAI_API_KEY:-}" ] && echo "OPENAI_API_KEY is set in shell env"`
96	    - If not in shell env, look for a project-local `.env`: `[ -f .env ] && grep -q '^OPENAI_API_KEY=' .env && echo "OPENAI_API_KEY is set in .env"` (don't print the value).
97	16. If neither check finds it: ask the user which provider they want to use (Anthropic / DeepSeek / OpenAI / etc.). Both extensions auto-load `.env` from `ctx.cwd` on `session_start` and tmux forwards env via `-e KEY=VAL`, so dropping the key into a project-local `.env` Just Works for both agents.
98	17. If `.env` does not exist, offer to create a stub with placeholder lines for common providers (commented out — user fills in real values themselves):
99	    ```
100	    # ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
101	    # DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=sk-...
102	    # OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
103	    ```
104	    Never write a real key to disk.
105	
106	### Step 7 — Final verification (no servers started)
107	
108	18. Run `cd apps/verifier && npx tsc --noEmit && cd ../..` — must exit 0. Confirms TypeScript compiles cleanly across both extensions and the shared substrate.
109	
110	### Step 8 — Report
111	
112	Present a status table per the Report section.
113	
114	## Report
115	
116	Present the install result in this format:
117	
118	```
119	Pi Verifier Agent — install ready
120	
121	  ── Critical prerequisites ──────────────────────
122	  node           ✓ v[version]
123	  pi             ✓ [version]
124	  tmux           ✓ [version]
125	
126	  ── Standard prerequisites ──────────────────────
127	  uv             ✓ [version]
128	  python3        ✓ [version]
129	  sqlite3        ✓ [version]
130	  just           ✓ [version]
131	
132	  ── Optional ────────────────────────────────────
133	  $TERM_PROGRAM  [value — recognized | falls back to Terminal.app]
134	
135	  ── Configuration ───────────────────────────────
136	  apps/verifier/node_modules/                    ✓
137	  .pi/settings.json (valid JSON)                 ✓
138	  .pi/verifier/agents/verify_sqlite.md           ✓
139	  .pi/verifier/scripts/verify_sqlite.py (+x)     ✓
140	  .pi/verifier/prompts/verify_on_stop.md         ✓
141	
142	  ── Provider key ────────────────────────────────
143	  [PROVIDER]_API_KEY   ✓ set in [shell env | .env]
144	
145	  ── Final verification ──────────────────────────
146	  npx tsc --noEmit  ✓ exit 0
147	
148	  Ready: [N]/[total] checks passing.
149	
150	  ── Next steps ──────────────────────────────────
151	  Prime a fresh agent session:     /prime
152	  Launch the verifier loop:        just vsql  (or `just v`, `just vpy`, `just vimg`)
153	  Or attach manually:              run `pi -e ./apps/verifier/verifiable.ts` and type `/verify` in the builder
154	```

## Instructions

- Run every check via Bash — do not assume anything is installed.
- Show a one-line pass/fail status after each check.
- Critical deps (`node`, `pi`, `tmux`) gate the install — stop and instruct the user if missing.
- For optional deps (`drive`, `WezTerm`, etc.) note absence but continue.
- For the API key step: confirm a provider key is set in either `process.env` or `.env`. **Never read or print key values** — only confirm presence.
- Do NOT start `pi`, do NOT run any `just v*` recipe, do NOT open windows — this command verifies readiness only.
- If a `.env` doesn't exist, offer to create one with the chosen provider's key as a placeholder (commented), but never write a real key.

## Workflow

### Step 1 — Critical prerequisites (gate)

If any of these are missing, stop and instruct the user before continuing.

1. Check `node`: `command -v node && node --version`. Need ≥ 20. If missing → `brew install node` (macOS) or use a Node version manager (nvm, fnm, volta).
2. Check `pi`: `command -v pi && pi --version`. The Pi Coding Agent CLI. If missing → `npm install -g @mariozechner/pi-coding-agent` (or the user's preferred install path; consult [Pi Coding Agent docs](https://github.com/mariozechner/pi-coding-agent)).
3. Check `tmux`: `command -v tmux && tmux -V`. Need 3.x+. If missing → `brew install tmux` (macOS) or `apt install tmux` (Debian/Ubuntu).

Stop and report each missing critical dep separately so the user can install incrementally.

### Step 2 — Standard prerequisites

These are all required by the verifier script or the `just` recipes; install missing ones via the listed commands.

4. Check `uv` (astral-uv — runs the SQLite verifier script with inline PEP 723 deps):
   `command -v uv && uv --version`. If missing → `curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh`.
5. Check `python3` (the verifier script's shebang resolves to `uv run --script` which uses Python ≥ 3.11):
   `command -v python3 && python3 --version`.
6. Check `sqlite3`: `command -v sqlite3 && sqlite3 --version`. Used internally by the verifier script for dot-commands like `.schema`.
7. Check `just`: `command -v just && just --version`. Optional but every workflow command in the README runs through justfile recipes — strongly recommended. If missing → `brew install just` (macOS) or [installation instructions](https://github.com/casey/just#installation).

### Step 3 — Optional environment notes

8. Detect terminal emulator: `echo "$TERM_PROGRAM"`. The launcher's per-emulator dispatch knows about Ghostty, iTerm, Apple_Terminal, WezTerm. If `$TERM_PROGRAM` is something else (e.g., `vscode`, `WarpTerminal`), the launcher falls back to a Terminal.app window via `osascript` — also fine.

### Step 4 — Install TypeScript dependencies

10. Run `cd apps/verifier && npm install`. This installs `@mariozechner/pi-coding-agent`, `@mariozechner/pi-tui`, `typebox`, `typescript`, `@types/node` into `apps/verifier/node_modules/`.

### Step 5 — Verify configuration files

11. Persona file exists and frontmatter is parseable:
    - `[ -f .pi/verifier/agents/verify_sqlite.md ] && echo persona-present`
    - The frontmatter must declare `name`, `description`, `tools`, `model`, `domain`, `bash_policy.{mode, allowed_script, runner}`, optionally `max_loops`. The exact contract is enforced at runtime by `apps/verifier/_shared/frontmatter.ts:parseVerifierPersona`.
12. Script file exists and is executable:
    - `[ -f .pi/verifier/scripts/verify_sqlite.py ] && [ -x .pi/verifier/scripts/verify_sqlite.py ] && echo script-executable`
    - If not executable: `chmod +x .pi/verifier/scripts/verify_sqlite.py`.
13. User-prompt template exists:
    - `[ -f .pi/verifier/prompts/verify_on_stop.md ] && echo prompt-template-present`
14. Project settings exist:
    - `[ -f .pi/settings.json ] && python3 -c 'import json; json.load(open(".pi/settings.json"))' && echo settings-valid-json`

### Step 6 — Verify environment / provider API key

15. Default model across all verifier personas is `openai/gpt-5.5` → the canonical key is `OPENAI_API_KEY`. Check it without printing the value:
    - `[ -n "${OPENAI_API_KEY:-}" ] && echo "OPENAI_API_KEY is set in shell env"`
    - If not in shell env, look for a project-local `.env`: `[ -f .env ] && grep -q '^OPENAI_API_KEY=' .env && echo "OPENAI_API_KEY is set in .env"` (don't print the value).
16. If neither check finds it: ask the user which provider they want to use (Anthropic / DeepSeek / OpenAI / etc.). Both extensions auto-load `.env` from `ctx.cwd` on `session_start` and tmux forwards env via `-e KEY=VAL`, so dropping the key into a project-local `.env` Just Works for both agents.
17. If `.env` does not exist, offer to create a stub with placeholder lines for common providers (commented out — user fills in real values themselves):
    ```
    # ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
    # DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=sk-...
    # OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
    ```
    Never write a real key to disk.

### Step 7 — Final verification (no servers started)

18. Run `cd apps/verifier && npx tsc --noEmit && cd ../..` — must exit 0. Confirms TypeScript compiles cleanly across both extensions and the shared substrate.

      {"level": "FEEDBACK", "meaning": "≥1 claim failed AND verifier_prompt was called — the system working as designed.", "bar": "orange"},

  "what_student_must_internalize": [
    "The verifier attacks the REVIEW constraint — one of the only two constraints (planning + reviewing) that bind agentic engineering. That's why it's high-leverage.",
    "Verification = decomposition. Break the builder's claims into atomic propositions and prove each against actual state with a deterministic tool. The agent's prose is a claim, never proof.",
    "You spend tokens to save time. 2–5× the tokens per turn is the correct trade when your time is the scarce resource.",
    "The verifier is the rare pattern that compounds trust AND scale simultaneously — most agentic moves trade one for the other.",
    "The un-promptable harness forces you to template your engineering: fixes go into the persona / script / prompt, never a one-off. That solves the whole class, not the instance.",
    "Read-only is enforced by architecture (three independent layers), not by asking the model nicely. Bash is the most dangerous tool — lock it to one script.",
    "It's AND, not OR: a builder model + a different verifier model beats either alone. Stack and orchestrate intelligence; benchmarks that test one model miss this.",
    "The builder never knows the verifier exists (top-down observer): lifecycle ticks over a socket, substance pulled from the session JSONL slice.",
    "Own your harness — that control is what makes the input lock, tool narrowing, bash policy, and auto-spawn possible; other tools change under your feet.",
    "The Report's 'what could you not verify / what do you need from me' is a flywheel: every gap is the next thing you template. Verifier accuracy compounds."
  ],

    "Trying to 'just tell the verifier' to fix a miss. Its input is locked by design — the only fix is editing the persona/script/template. Fighting the lock misses the lesson.",

1	# TAC-1 · Hello Agentic Coding — Master Teaching Notes
2	
3	> Source of truth for the expanded chapter. Video 21:51 · Beginner · Tactic #1: **Stop Coding**
4	> Lesson artifact: a 35-line README, one settings file, and three ~20-line launcher scripts. That's the whole codebase, on purpose.
5	
6	**Lesson thesis in one sentence:** AI coding (generating code from prompts) was phase one; agentic coding — prompts that reliably execute long chains of tools inside a programmable agent — is phase two, and the engineer who commands it becomes irreplaceable by replacing themselves.
7	
8	**The chapter must land eight ideas.** Each below follows: Hook → Picture → Worked example (course codebase) → Dan's term → Failure mode → Retrieval Q.
9	
10	---
11	
12	## Idea 1 — A new role exists: the Agentic Engineer
13	
14	**Hook.** In 2023, before it was obvious, Dan bought a domain name as a bet: agenticengineer.com. The bet was that a new software role would emerge, defined not by writing code but by *building systems that can take actions as we can*. Lesson 1 opens by declaring the bet settled: the role now exists, and this course exists to move you into it.
15	
16	**Picture.** Frame t0078 (1:18): the agenticengineer.com page on screen while Dan narrates the 2023 prediction. Frame t0115 (1:55): the two-phase timeline — Phase 1 "AI CODING" (vibe coders born, code commoditized) flowing into Phase 2 "AGENTIC CODING" (real engineers strike back).
17	
18	**Worked example.** The entire lesson repo *is* the role in miniature: nothing in `tac/tac-1` is application code. It's a README of prompts, a permissions file, and launchers — artifacts of someone who directs systems rather than types programs.
19	
20	**Dan's term.** *Phase two Agentic Engineer.* Also the era framing: *"In the generative AI age, AI coding was phase one... Agentic coding marks phase two. This is where real engineers strike back."*
21	
22	**Failure mode.** Hearing "new role" as a title change rather than a job change. The weak student keeps doing phase-1 work (prompt → code → paste) with a new label. The role's actual definition — building systems that take actions — is testable: if nothing runs without you pressing the keys, you're still phase one.
23	
24	**Retrieval Q.** What defines the agentic engineer role, in Dan's 2023 prediction wording? *(Building systems that can take actions as we can.)*
25	
26	---
27	
28	## Idea 2 — The mission: become the engineer they can't replace
29

**Retrieval Q.** Name Claude Code's three essential elements and the claim they justify. *(Reasoning model + consistent long tool chains + right agent architecture; reliable agentic coding at scale wasn't possible before it.)*

---

## Idea 7 — Programmable agentic coding: the agent as a function call

**Hook.** The lesson's biggest unlock is almost a throwaway line: Claude Code runs in the terminal. Which means any programming language with terminal access can *call it*. Which means the agent is no longer an app you sit in front of — it's a component you build with.

**Picture.** Frame t1063 (17:43): the `programmable/` directory — three launchers + `prompt.md`. Frame t1105 (18:25): `programmable.py` on screen, ~30 lines. Frame t1205 (20:05): the headless run's final REPORT in the terminal. Frame t1000 (16:40): the README-35-lines shot that frames this whole section.

**Worked example.** All three launchers are the same five steps in different costumes — read `programmable/prompt.md`, pass it to `claude -p`, capture output, print it, propagate errors:

- `programmable.sh` — `PROMPT_CONTENT="$(cat programmable/prompt.md)"; OUTPUT="$(claude -p "$PROMPT_CONTENT")"; echo "$OUTPUT"` (3 lines; the pattern with nothing else)
- `programmable.py` — `subprocess.run(["claude", "-p", prompt_content], capture_output=True, text=True)`, print stdout/stderr, `sys.exit(returncode)` (the variant Dan runs; the most production-shaped: error handling + exit-code propagation)
- `programmable.ts` — Bun: `await $\`claude -p ${promptContent}\`.text()` then log (proves language choice is irrelevant)

`prompt.md` itself is a *superset* of the README demo and self-contained: it creates BOTH `main_aic.py` and `main_tac.py` (no dependency on a prior interactive run), and adds a fourth block the README prompt lacks — `REPORT: respond with the exact output of both .py files`. That REPORT block is the seed of every report-back/verification pattern in later AI developer workflows: headless runs must *tell you what happened*.

Demo order matters and is worth reproducing exactly: delete the branch from the interactive run first (`git branch -D demo-agentic-coding`), then `uv run python programmable/programmable.py` from `main` — and watch the whole workflow re-materialize without you.

**Dan's term.** *Programmable agentic coding* / a *programmable agentic coding tool*. Why it matters: "we can embed our own agents, our own workflows, our own agentic prompts across the software development lifecycle" — across all developer environments, "including full agentic environments where we're not even present," with *agentic triggers* (a later-course topic) deciding when they fire. "It's not just about the agentic prompt. It's about **where** we can use the agentic prompt."

**Failure mode.** Watching instead of running — the scripts look too trivial to bother with, so the student never feels the qualitative difference between *chatting with* an agent and *invoking* one. Second failure: missing that `prompt.md` ≠ the README prompt (the superset + REPORT differences are exactly the parts that make headless runs viable). Third: not realizing `.env.sample` (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=`) marks the API-billing path that headless/CI usage implies.

**Retrieval Q.** What one property of Claude Code makes it programmable, and what does prompt.md's REPORT block demand? *(It runs in the terminal, so any language with terminal access can invoke `claude -p`; REPORT demands the exact output of both .py files.)*

---

## Idea 8 — The contradicting truth: replace yourself

**Hook.** The lesson ends on a paradox sharp enough to be the course's motto: *to become an irreplaceable engineer, you will replace yourself.* The engineer who automates their own work owns the automation — and no vibe coder will replicate what that engineer can do.

**Picture.** t1250 (20:50) is B-roll (hands typing) — render this beat as a designed pull-quote, not a frame (`diagram_instead: true` in the frame plan).

**Worked example.** Lesson 1's arc in miniature already performed it: the engineer ran a prompt interactively (doing the work), then scripted the same prompt (`programmable/*`), making themselves unnecessary for that workflow — permanently. Multiply by every workflow you own: that's the course.

**Dan's term.** *The contradicting truth.* Supporting frame: evolution — "Evolution forces us to leave skills behind to adapt new ones and bet on potential futures. But in the tech industry, this is where all the alpha lies... your asymmetric engineering advantage exists... in the future." Teaser for lesson 2: leverage points such that *10 minutes of your work equals 60+ minutes of another engineer's*.

**Failure mode.** Reading the paradox as job-loss fatalism (and disengaging) instead of as the leverage strategy it is. The resolution the student must be able to articulate: what gets replaced is your *typing*; what becomes irreplaceable is your *judgment about what to build and your ownership of the systems that build it*.

**Retrieval Q.** State the contradicting truth and resolve it in one sentence. *(To become irreplaceable you'll replace yourself — you automate your current work, and the irreplaceable part becomes your command of the systems doing it.)*

---

- **TAC** — Tactical Agentic Coding (8 lessons, 8 tactics, one codebase each; per-lesson **loot box** of prompts/links/assets under the video)

1	# TAC-1 — Outdated vs Current (course era → mid-2026)
2	
3	TAC-1 ages unusually well because it teaches primitives, and Dan future-proofs on camera: *"Your Claude Code UI might look different. You might be using newer models. That's all great... Don't let that distract you from the value embedded in each lesson."* Still, five things have moved. For each: what the course shows, what current practice is, and whether the book needs an overlay.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## 1. Reusable agent behavior: prompt files → Agent Skills  ⟵ the big named gap
8	
9	**Course era:** reusable behavior is encoded as a raw prompt file (`programmable/prompt.md`) plus launcher scripts. Works, but discovery, triggering, and composition are all manual.
10	**Current:** Agent Skills are the first-class encoding — `SKILL.md` files with frontmatter (name, description, trigger guidance), loaded on demand by Claude Code and shareable across projects/teams. Skills are the modern answer to "how do I package the thing my agent knows how to do?" — exactly the question `programmable/` answers primitively.
11	**Book treatment:** overlay REQUIRED. This is the course's most-cited gap ("Skills as modern encoding of engineering"). Teach prompt.md first (pedagogically perfect: no magic), then show the same workflow as a Skill.
12	**Overlay:** `X2ciJedw2vU` — *RAW Agentic Coding: ZERO to Agent SKILL* (include_in_phase1: **yes**).
13	
14	## 2. Embedding: bare `claude -p` → headless mode + Claude Agent SDK
15	
16	**Course era:** `claude -p "<prompt>"` via subprocess from sh/ts/py; output captured as plain text; REPORT requested inside the prompt itself.
17	**Current:** the pattern survives verbatim (and remains the best teaching form), but production embedding now uses headless flags — `--output-format json|stream-json`, `--allowedTools`, `--permission-mode`, session resume — and, for real systems, the Claude Agent SDK (Python/TS): structured outputs, hooks, subagents, multi-turn control. What TAC-1 calls "programmable agentic coding" grew into a supported product surface.
18	**Book treatment:** sidebar ("the 3-line script you just wrote has a grown-up form"), not a rewrite — concept unchanged: agent as callable component.
19	**Overlay:** `6fCqj4xFCZI` — *How Claude Code CHANGED Engineering Forever* (include_in_phase1: **yes**).
20	
21	## 3. Permissions: flat allowlist → modes, hooks, sandboxing
22	
23	**Course era:** `.claude/settings.json` with a flat `permissions.allow` list (`Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Bash(uv run:*)`, four git patterns, `WebSearch`).
24	**Current:** that syntax still works, but the surface grew: permission modes (plan/accept-edits/etc.), pre/post tool-use hooks, sandboxed bash, deny rules, and settings layering (user/project/local). Teams gate agents with hooks, not just allowlists.
25	**Book treatment:** footnote + "current practice" callout. The lesson's HABIT — always read what the agent may do before running it — transfers unchanged and is the actual teaching point.
26	**Overlay:** none needed.
27	
28	## 4. Models & UI: period detail, pre-handled by Dan
29	
30	**Course era:** course-era Claude models and TUI; Aider cited as the phase-1 analogue.
31	**Current:** newer model families (Claude 4.x → Claude 5 era), richer TUI, plan modes, background tasks. None of it invalidates a frame of the lesson — the demo is deliberately primitive-level.
32	**Book treatment:** one-line margin note on affected screenshots ("UI is period detail; the flow is identical today"). No overlay.
33	
34	## 5. Scale: one serial loop → fleets, subagents, parallel worktrees
35	
36	**Course era:** one agent, one workflow, serially, in one terminal — deliberately, since it's lesson 1 of 8.
37	**Current:** the same agentic prompt is routinely fanned out: subagents, background tasks, git-worktree-isolated parallel runs, orchestrated pipelines. "Systems that build systems" now has industrial-strength machinery.
38	**Book treatment:** forward-pointer only ("the course scales this in later lessons; today's ceiling is higher still"). Overlaying scale content on lesson 1 would front-run the pedagogy.
39	**Overlay candidates (deferred to later chapters):** `fop_yxV-mPo` — *Codebase Singularity*; `hGg3nWp7afg` — *3 Codebase Folders* (both include_in_phase1: **no**).
40	
41	---
42	
43	## What has NOT aged (teach with full confidence)
44	
45	- The phase-1/phase-2 frame and "AI coding is not enough" — if anything, more consensus now than at recording.
46	- The core four. Context/model/prompt/tools remains the complete diagnostic vocabulary for agentic failures.
47	- The agentic prompt as workflow-specification (RUN/CREATE/RUN/REPORT) — this shape is now everywhere (slash commands, skills, CI prompts).
48	- "Scale and performance, not novelty" as the right lens on tool calling.
49	- The three-essential-elements checklist for evaluating agentic tools.
50	- Terminal ubiquity as the embedding superpower.
51	- Report-back as the first closed-loop habit.
52	- The economics: token spend as pay-to-play. (Costs shifted; the logic didn't.)
53	
54	## Phase-1 overlay decision (strict, per brief: max 1–3)
55	
56	| # | Video | Maps to | Include |
57	|---|---|---|---|
58	| 1 | `2TIXl2rlA6Q` — AI Coding is NOT ENOUGH | operationalizes tactic (lesson thesis, phase model) | ✅ |
59	| 2 | `6fCqj4xFCZI` — How Claude Code CHANGED Engineering Forever | named hole (form factor + programmable embedding, current state) | ✅ |
60	| 3 | `X2ciJedw2vU` — RAW Agentic Coding: ZERO to Agent SKILL | corrects outdated (skills gap) | ✅ |
61	| 4 | `fop_yxV-mPo` — Codebase Singularity | self-operating vision → later lessons | ❌ defer |
62	| 5 | `hGg3nWp7afg` — 3 Codebase Folders | context engineering → later lessons | ❌ defer |
63
